title.narrative: Provision of emergency shelter support, and protection services to vulnerable returnees and host communities in high return areas

description.narrative: The recent developments in Syria after 27 November 2024 led to large-scale displacement. Multiple overlapping population movements continue in Syria, including new internal displacement within Syria, refugee and IDP returns, and movements out of Syria. UNHCR estimates that from 8 December 2024 to 23mid-January 2025, around 210,000 Syrians have returned to Syria, bringing the total number of returns since January 2024 to approximately 566,000. Out of the estimated 1.1 million Syrians internally displaced by hostilities at the end of November, more than half remained displaced and some 523,000 have already returned to their areas of origin. The hostilities also caused additional destruction of homes and infrastructure which were already damaged during the 14-year long conflict. Shelter assistance: The recent analysis shows the need for shelter assistance has significantly increased compared to the long-standing shelter needs of long-term displaced people. This new context presents new criticalities as well as the opportunity to broaden the UN humanitarian response.Two key developments are: the improved access for humanitarian organizations across a wider geographical area within a comprehensive Syria-wide approach, and the potential for many displaced persons to start returning to their places of origin. Many people have experienced multiple displacements, and their conditions remain dire. The proposed interventions aim to deliver a comprehensive and targeted emergency response that prioritizes shelter repair and rehabilitation to support the most vulnerable populations. By leveraging a coordinated and context-sensitive approach, this project will contribute to restoring safety, dignity and basic living conditions for 850 households (4,250 individuals), while ensuring alignment with inter-agency standard and best practices. UNHCR is adapting its rehabilitation and repair programmes to support both host communities and returnees, while maintaining a focus on areas affected by years of conflict, particularly the recent clashes and destruction caused by land and air attacks by various actors in Syria.The proposed interventions will cover: 1. Minor shelter repairs: this includes repairs to minor damage affecting roofs, non-structural walls, doors, windows, and basic water, sanitation and electrical systems within housing units.2. Rehabilitation of damaged houses: this covers repairs of more significant, yet manageable, structural and non-structural damage to residential housing, including single or multi-story buildings. Eligible housing types also include partially damaged or unfinished structures, as well as commercial or premises convertible for shelter use. Protection: Protection remains an essential need for displaced people, returnees and host communities. UNHCR has been scaling up its activities to address the needs of displaced, returnees and host communities by building on the existing networks, including UNHCR-supported community centres, outreach volunteers, and mobile units. Outreach volunteers play a fundamental role in identifying new arrivals’ needs, informing them of services, and referring cases to appropriate service providers. With the support of CERF, UNHCR plans to recruit additional outreach volunteers and equip them with ICT tools to conduct protection monitoring. UNHCR will also increase the number of lawyers and legal outreach volunteers to provide legal counselling and legal support. In total 2,400 people will benefit from legal support.
